newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Australia gas deregulation faces upstream hurdle.
newsitem.headline: Australia gas deregulation faces upstream hurdle.

text.p: Australia's ability to create upstream competition in the Victoria gas market through deregulation is hindered by a virtual monopoly position of Esso-BHP, an analyst's report said on Wednesday.

Esso Australia, a unit of U.S. oil giant Exxon Corp, and The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd, are 50/50 joint venture partners in the Bass Strait oil and gas fields, energy analyst Wood Mackenzie said in its April 1997 Australasia report.
The Bass Strait accounts for 68 percent of uncommitted gas reserves that could supply Victoria when the interstate gas grid is in place, so is likely to be the dominant supplier, the report said.

The state government plans to fully deregulate the gas market by 2001. Gas sales to Victoria currently range from 190 to 235 petajoules (PJ) per year (174 to 216 billion cubic feet), with demand rising two percent a year.
Producers other than Esso-BHP will for the first time be able to supply the state and new marketing companies will be able to offer the gas for sale to end users, Wood Mackenzie said.
But the huge reserves Bass Strait could apply to the Victoria market means it will be in a dominant position, the report said.
Wood Mackenzie said Bass Strait had only committed 1,800 PJ of its reserves, leaving 4,800 PJ uncommitted.

"While downstream competition between pipeline operators and gas distribution companies can be introduced through government restructure and privatisation of the business units, the ability to create upstream competition in the industry is hindered by the virtual monopoly reserves position of Esso/BHP in the Bass Strait," the report said.
Other potential fields that could supply Victoria include Yolla, Southwest Queensland Gas Unit, Sole, Patricia/Baleen, Minerva and Golden Beach.
But the fields all have uncommitted reserves of less than 10 percent, or a combined 2,140 PJ.
"Key to their entry will be the ability to develop the reserves and necessary infrastructure to be cost competitive with Bass Strait gas," the report said.

The analyst said Southwest Queensland possibly had the best chance to compete. The onshore field -- part of the Cooper Basin development -- has most of its gas gathering and gas transportation structure in place.
"Hence the region can potentially compete with low cost Bass Strait gas," the report said.
